Tuberculosis (TB) patients who are known to be HIV-positive or those living in settings with a high prevalence of HIV should receive a treatment regimen based on rifampicin (or rifabutin) for a minimum of six months. The optimal dosing frequency for this treatment is daily during both the intensive and continuation phases. 2. Co-occurring conditions such as hepatitis B or C should not be considered contraindications for initiating HIV or TB treatment in people who inject drugs (PWID). Similarly, alcohol dependence, active drug use, or mental health disorders should not be used as reasons to withhold treatment. 3. For patients with TB, viral hepatitis, or HIV who also have opioid dependence, opioid agonist therapy should be provided alongside medical treatment. There is no need to delay the initiation of anti-TB medication, hepatitis treatment, or antiretroviral therapy (ART) until the patient achieves abstinence from opioids. 4. The Xpert MTB/RIF test, recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO), is an automated, cartridge-based, real-time DNA test capable of detecting both TB and rifampicin resistance within two hours. It is more sensitive than microscopy for detecting TB in people living with HIV and can rapidly identify rifampicin resistance, significantly reducing the time to diagnose and treat multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB). 5. Collaborative TB and HIV services should be integrated into a comprehensive care package for PWID. TB is the most common AIDS-defining illness in this population, and recognizing TB symptoms may often be the first indication of HIV infection. Intensified TB case-finding, leading to timely access to TB treatment and ART, reduces mortality and interrupts TB transmission. 6. All PWID living with HIV should be regularly screened for TB using a clinical symptom-based tool that assesses for current cough, fever, weight loss, or night sweats. This screening should occur at the time of initial HIV care presentation and during every subsequent encounter with healthcare or outreach workers. Those reporting any of these symptoms should undergo further evaluation for active TB and other diseases. 7. Diagnostic workups for TB should follow national guidelines and sound clinical practices to confirm active TB or establish an alternative diagnosis. Regular TB screening is essential, regardless of whether the individual has received or is receiving isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) or ART. 8. In settings where the general population TB prevalence is 100 per 100,000 or higher, WHO recommends systematic screening for active TB among select high-risk groups, including PWID, irrespective of their HIV status. 9. Governmental and non-governmental organizations providing services to PWID play a critical role in early TB identification and timely treatment or prevention. This includes settings such as opioid substitution therapy (OST) clinics or drop-in centers. 10. WHO strongly recommends using Xpert MTB/RIF as the primary diagnostic test for individuals suspected of having MDR-TB, those living with HIV who exhibit TB symptoms, or those with unknown HIV status but strong clinical evidence of HIV infection. 11. For adults and children presumed to have pulmonary TB but not at risk for MDR-TB or HIV-related TB, Xpert MTB/RIF may also be used as the initial diagnostic test, depending on available resources. 12. Smear-negative pulmonary and extrapulmonary TB are common among people living with HIV and are associated with poor treatment outcomes and high early mortality. If extrapulmonary TB is suspected, diagnostic processes should be expedited using all available and appropriate investigations, including clinical assessment, Xpert MTB/RIF, mycobacterial culture, and chest X-ray. 13. In high HIV-prevalence settings, presumptive anti-TB treatment should be initiated in seriously ill patients when investigations are negative, and there is no improvement with broad-spectrum parenteral antibiotics. 14. Maintaining confidentiality during contact investigations can be challenging due to social connections among index cases and their contacts, particularly in shared community settings. All individuals should be treated with respect, and confidentiality must be upheld in accordance with program guidelines. 15. Early initiation of TB treatment is critical for saving lives and preventing further transmission. Medical staff may hesitate to start treatment for PWID due to concerns about poor adherence, medication interactions, and adverse effects, particularly those related to viral hepatitis treatment. However, adequately supported PWID can achieve adherence and clinical outcomes comparable to those of non-drug users. 16. Health services for PWID should ensure access to appropriate treatment by adhering to current national clinical guidelines. Collaboration is essential to supervise treatment while simplifying its delivery on an outpatient basis whenever possible. 17. TB treatment should ideally be integrated with HIV care and treatment, providing access to sterile injecting equipment, drug dependence treatment, and other medications to minimize the need for multiple visits. 18. Ambulatory TB care should be prioritized over hospitalization, which should be reserved for cases with medical indications. Continuity of care, including OST and ART, must be maintained during hospitalization to prevent loss to follow-up and withdrawal-related barriers to seeking care. 19. PWID living with HIV or those newly diagnosed with drug-sensitive TB should receive the standard first-line TB regimen, consisting of two months of isoniazid, rifampicin/rifabutin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, followed by four months of rifampicin/rifabutin and isoniazid on a daily schedule. 20. Patients with drug-sensitive TB and conditions such as hepatitis virus carriage, a history of acute hepatitis, or current excessive alcohol consumption can also receive the standard first-line TB regimen, provided there is no clinical evidence of chronic liver disease. However, hepatotoxic reactions to anti-TB drugs may be more common in these patients and should be anticipated. 21. Patients with unstable or advanced liver disease should undergo liver function testing at the start of treatment, if possible. 22. PWID with a history of TB treatment interruption or incarceration may be at higher risk for MDR-TB. Patients with both HIV and MDR-TB face complex clinical management, limited treatment options, and poor outcomes. 23. Seriously ill patients should be offered palliative care, including access to essential medicines such as opioids for pain management, to ensure minimal suffering and dignity even when curative treatments are no longer viable. 24. Barriers to TB treatment adherence vary between settings and individuals. Services should consult with PWID to identify effective strategies to overcome these barriers and develop locally appropriate solutions. 25. Evidence suggests that adherence improves with directly observed therapy, adherence reminders, peer counseling, contingency management, monetary incentives, and an integrated care package that includes OST and addresses psychosocial and healthcare needs. 26. For latent TB infection (LTBI), adults and adolescents living with HIV should be screened using a clinical algorithm. Those without symptoms of active TB should be offered IPT, regardless of their degree of immunosuppression, ART status, or previous TB treatment history. 27. In high TB prevalence settings, continuous IPT for at least 36 months reduces the risk of developing active TB by 38% compared to six months of IPT. Continuous IPT provides additional protection for people living with HIV who are on ART. 28. Isoniazid is effective and well-tolerated among PWID, including those co-infected with hepatitis B or C, provided liver function is monitored.
